column1: # The settings registry: every DM_* switch the core reads (docs/ARCHITECTURE.md, Settings). One row a switch, tab-separated:
#   name   type (bool, int, float, hex, str)   default ("" = unset: the code decides; see its doc)   scope   when   read in   doc
# scope: profile = a game profile may set it (android.tsv env rows); porter = the porter writes it to env.txt; app = the Android app sets it (its folders, the player's settings);
#        debug = for bring-up and diagnosis only (a profile may not set it; promote it to profile first). ",ios" = read only by the iOS host.
# when: start = read once at start-up; live = re-read while the game runs (a ctl.txt `env` line changes it); ? = not documented yet.
# tests/test_settings.py checks that every getenv("DM_...") in the core has a row here and that profiles and porter set only rows they may.

column7: the adaptive frame-rate governor (perf_android.c); 0 = off, the game runs at its own rate
the governor steps up a rate when frames fit in this percent of the faster rate's budget (1..99)
the folder of the add-on content (DLC) the porter installed
silent sink (Android defaults to real output)
diagnostic: the whole real-output path (AudioUnit callback pacing, background take-over) but with the output silenced (lifecycle tests on the Mac without noise)

catch-up frames (a frame rendered on the updating thread when nothing was rendered since the last update) only while fewer than this many frames have been rendered; unset: always. For games that update several times per renderer event and stream from looping voice buffers (Fire Emblem: Three Houses: 200)

writes every block the renderer hands to the output, in play order (stereo int16, 48 kHz), to this file; logs the blocks that rendered nothing and those from the catch-up queue (`audren dump:`); devtools/pcm_glitches.py finds clicks, gaps and clipping in it

logs the first 200 renderer updates with the frames rendered since the previous one, and the next 300 catch-up frames (`audren: catch-up at update …`): the calling thread, the time since the previous update and the frames queued ahead. Animal Crossing: New Horizons: 14-25 catch-ups a second with or
the control file of a development build (ctl.txt: key presses, env lines, shots); release builds ignore it
diagnostic: on the Mac, make the sound card callback ask N frames each time (1024 = the iOS default, reproduces the crackling)

the host's dynamic resolution: a level for a profile's env row, `low` (lowest scale 0.85 against 90% of the frame time), `medium` (0.70, 85%) or `high` (0.50, 80%), or a number, the lowest scale (0.5 to 0.95, 85% budget); 0 or unset = off. In a game with a render-scale stub: every 30 frames held at the cap, GPU p90 over the budget lowers the scale 0.05, under 70% of it raises it (Tears of the Kingdom's pond: 1.0 -> 0.6 saved only 2.6 ms of GPU p90). In a game without one (no state page) it steers the engine's own dynamic resolution: the GPU clock the game reads (nvnDeviceGetTimestampInNanoseconds, GetCurrentTimestampInNanoseconds) runs k times as fast, k between 1 and 1 / (lowest scale)², raised 15% while GPU p90 is over the budget and lowered under 70% of it, the budget taken at 30 fps under a 30 fps ceiling (hle_nvn.c engine_dyn_tick). Only for engines whose resolution controller reads NVN counter timestamps (Pokémon Scarlet / Violet); a game that paces frames on them would be thrown off
the iOS launcher: the keys an env file set (Launcher.swift keeps them)
the 30 fps ceiling of the profile (fps_ceiling) when 30; 0 lifts it. Default: the profile
off = no frame hold; any other value holds. Default: the profile (fps_hold)
a fpslock.tsv the porter wrote (FPSLocker rows for this build) when the host has none
pin the governor at 60, 40 or 30 fps; 0 = no pin
the frame rate the game is held to; 0 = the game's own. Default: the profile (fps_target)
line-buffered: runs end at the time-limit alarm or a crash, which never flush stdio
